options.a: Flexibility and muscular strength first, then cardio and resting measures
options.b: Resting measures, body composition, cardio, muscular fitness, flexibility
options.c: Muscular strength first, then resting HR and BP, then the cardio test
options.d: Cardiorespiratory test first, then body composition and resting BP

distractorExplanations.a: Resting HR and BP must be taken before exercise raises them, so they come first, not last.
distractorExplanations.c: Strength testing first raises HR and BP and fatigues the client before the cardio test.
distractorExplanations.d: A cardio test first raises HR and BP and can distort body-composition readings such as BIA.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-001.prompt: When several fitness assessments are done in one session, which order does ACSM generally recommend?
acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-001.explanation: ACSM's Guidelines suggest resting HR, BP, and body composition first, then cardiorespiratory fitness, then muscular fitness, with flexibility last, so earlier tests do not distort later ones.

options.a: An estimated one-repetition maximum for the back squat
options.b: Body fat percentage without any other measurements
options.c: A cardiorespiratory baseline and intensity reference
options.d: Bone mineral density and long-term fracture risk

distractorExplanations.a: A 1RM needs strength testing or prediction from submaximal lifts; resting HR gives no strength data.
distractorExplanations.b: Body fat needs skinfolds, BIA, or another composition method.
distractorExplanations.d: Bone density requires DXA imaging, not a heart rate reading.

options.a: Weak hip abductors and external rotators, such as gluteus medius
options.b: Weak ankle plantar flexors, such as the soleus and gastrocnemius
options.c: Tight hamstrings pulling the pelvis into a posterior tilt
options.d: Weak quadriceps that cannot extend the knee under load

distractorExplanations.b: Weak plantar flexors do not pull the knees inward; valgus is a frontal-plane hip control problem.
distractorExplanations.c: Posterior pelvic tilt from tight hamstrings shows as a rounded low back, not knees caving in.
distractorExplanations.d: Quadriceps weakness limits depth or knee extension, but does not by itself drive the knees medially.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-004.prompt: Knee valgus (knees caving in) during a squat is most commonly linked to:

options.a: Estimate VO2max before a laboratory treadmill test
options.b: Screen for health risks and flag need for medical clearance
options.c: Replace the informed consent form before training begins
options.d: Classify the client's fitness level for program design

distractorExplanations.a: The PAR-Q+ is a questionnaire; it does not estimate aerobic capacity.
distractorExplanations.c: Screening and informed consent are separate documents; one does not replace the other.
distractorExplanations.d: Fitness level comes from assessments, not from a health-risk questionnaire.

options.a: Upper-arm skinfold at the triceps only
options.b: Resting heart rate taken at the wrist
options.c: Waist, with other sites per protocol
options.d: Chest girth measured at full inhalation

distractorExplanations.a: Triceps skinfold is a skinfold site, not a circumference site.
distractorExplanations.b: Resting heart rate is a cardiovascular measure, not a body-composition circumference.
distractorExplanations.d: Circumference protocols measure at end of normal exhalation, and chest girth is not a standard formula site.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-006.prompt: Which site is commonly included in circumference-based body composition formulas?

options.a: Weak upper trapezius that cannot hold the scapula up
options.b: Tight rhomboids pulling the scapulae toward the spine
options.c: Weak latissimus dorsi failing to control shoulder flexion
options.d: Upper trapezius and levator scapulae dominating the lift

distractorExplanations.a: Shoulder elevation means the upper trapezius is overworking, not weak.
distractorExplanations.b: Tight rhomboids retract the scapulae; they do not cause shrugging during a push.
distractorExplanations.c: The lats depress and extend the shoulder; weak lats do not explain the shoulders rising.

options.a: Uncontrolled hypertension may need clearance and lower intensity
options.b: Blood pressure sets the exact target heart rate for the session
options.c: Low blood pressure always rules out resistance training that day
options.d: A single reading is enough to diagnose the client with hypertension

distractorExplanations.b: Target heart rate comes from HRmax or HRR methods, not from a BP reading.
distractorExplanations.c: Low readings warrant symptom checks, but they do not automatically rule out training.
distractorExplanations.d: Trainers do not diagnose; hypertension is diagnosed by a clinician from repeated readings.

options.a: Lower-body muscular endurance from repeated stepping
options.b: Aerobic fitness from 1-mile walk time and heart rate
options.c: Hamstring and low-back flexibility after a warm-up
options.d: Walking gait mechanics and ankle range of motion

distractorExplanations.a: The test uses walk time and heart rate to estimate VO2, not leg muscular endurance.
distractorExplanations.c: Flexibility is measured with tests such as sit-and-reach, not a timed walk.
distractorExplanations.d: Gait observation is not scored; the Rockport result is an aerobic estimate.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-009.prompt: The Rockport 1-mile walk test is primarily used to estimate:

options.a: Tight chest and upper trapezius with weak deep neck flexors
options.b: Tight hamstrings and glutes with weak hip flexors
options.c: Tight hip flexors and low back with weak glutes and abs
options.d: Weak erector spinae with tight abdominals and glutes

distractorExplanations.a: Tight chest and upper traps with weak neck flexors is upper crossed syndrome.
distractorExplanations.b: Tight hamstrings and glutes pull the pelvis into posterior tilt, the opposite pattern.
distractorExplanations.d: This reverses the pattern: in lower crossed syndrome the erectors are tight and the abs weak.

options.a: Reduce the load and continue if the pain eases
options.b: Switch to the same movement on a machine
options.c: Apply ice and resume after a short rest break
options.d: Stop the movement and refer for medical review

distractorExplanations.a: Sharp joint pain is a stop signal, not something to train around with lighter load.
distractorExplanations.b: Changing equipment still loads the painful joint without knowing the cause.
distractorExplanations.c: Resuming after ice ignores a red-flag symptom that needs evaluation.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-011.prompt: A client reports sharp joint pain during an assessment. The trainer should:

options.a: Whether the client already exercises regularly
options.b: The client's resting blood pressure category
options.c: The number of CVD risk factors the client has
options.d: The client's age and body mass index category

distractorExplanations.b: BP is useful data, but the current algorithm does not start from BP category.
distractorExplanations.c: Risk-factor counting was removed from the ACSM algorithm in 2015.
distractorExplanations.d: Age and BMI are not decision points in the current preparticipation algorithm.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-012.prompt: The current ACSM preparticipation screening algorithm first considers:
acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-012.explanation: Since 2015, ACSM screening starts with whether the client currently exercises, then looks at known cardiovascular, metabolic, or renal disease, signs or symptoms, and the desired intensity.

options.a: Toes pointing straight ahead through the rep
options.b: Knee valgus, hip drop, or trunk lean
options.c: Arms held level with the shoulders
options.d: Heel of the standing foot flat on the floor

distractorExplanations.a: A neutral foot position is the goal, not a compensation.
distractorExplanations.c: Level arms are part of the test setup, not a fault.
distractorExplanations.d: A flat standing heel is expected; heel lift would be the compensation.

options.a: A direct measure of body fat and visceral fat
options.b: Weight relative to waist circumference
options.c: Weight relative to height, not body fat
options.d: An estimate of lean mass from height alone

distractorExplanations.a: BMI does not measure fat directly; muscular people can score as overweight.
distractorExplanations.b: Waist circumference is a separate measure; BMI uses weight and height.
distractorExplanations.d: BMI does not estimate lean mass and uses weight, not height alone.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-014.explanation: BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. It screens weight category risk but cannot separate fat from lean mass, so athletes and older adults may be misclassified.

options.a: Tight calves or hip flexors with a weak posterior chain
options.b: Tight hamstrings with weak hip flexors and quadriceps
options.c: Weak calves with overactive tibialis anterior muscles
options.d: Tight latissimus dorsi with weak abdominal muscles

distractorExplanations.b: Tight hamstrings pull the pelvis back; they do not cause excessive forward lean.
distractorExplanations.c: Weak calves and an overactive tibialis would ease dorsiflexion, not limit it.
distractorExplanations.d: Tight lats cause the arms to fall forward, not the trunk to lean excessively.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-015.prompt: During an overhead squat, excessive forward trunk lean most commonly suggests:

options.a: Complete two weeks of steady-state cardio without pain
options.b: Perform bodyweight squats at a fast, continuous tempo
options.c: Show adequate strength and controlled landing mechanics
options.d: Hold a static stretch for 30 seconds at each major joint

distractorExplanations.a: Aerobic base does not show the strength and landing control that impact drills need.
distractorExplanations.b: Fast squats show little about absorbing landing forces.
distractorExplanations.d: Flexibility alone does not prepare joints for impact loading.

options.a: About 30–60 seconds between sets
options.b: About 60–90 seconds between sets
options.c: About 90–120 seconds between sets
options.d: About 3–5 minutes between sets

distractorExplanations.a: Short rest suits muscular endurance, not maximal strength.
distractorExplanations.b: This rest range is typical of hypertrophy work.
distractorExplanations.c: Two minutes may not fully restore phosphocreatine for heavy sets near maximum.

options.a: Box or bodyweight squat, then goblet squat, then barbell
options.b: Barbell back squat first, then goblet squat, then box squat
options.c: Split squat first, then pistol squat, then barbell squat
options.d: Leg press only until the client can lift bodyweight twice

distractorExplanations.b: Starting with a loaded barbell skips pattern learning; progress from simpler to harder.
distractorExplanations.c: A pistol squat is an advanced single-leg skill and a poor second step.
distractorExplanations.d: Machine strength does not teach the free squat pattern, and this criterion is arbitrary.

options.a: Increasing load every session regardless of form
options.b: Gradually raising load, volume, or complexity
options.c: Keeping the same program to master technique
options.d: Adding sets until the client reaches exhaustion

distractorExplanations.a: Adding load regardless of form invites injury; overload must stay within recovery and technique.
distractorExplanations.c: An unchanged program stops producing adaptation once the body adjusts.
distractorExplanations.d: Training to exhaustion every session is not progressive overload and hurts recovery.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-programming-004.prompt: Which statement best describes progressive overload?

options.a: It burns more calories per session than aerobic training
options.b: It allows spot reduction of fat from the trained muscles
options.c: It helps preserve lean mass during a calorie deficit
options.d: It removes the need to track diet while losing weight

distractorExplanations.a: Steady aerobic work usually burns more calories per session than typical lifting.
distractorExplanations.b: Spot reduction is a myth; fat loss happens across the whole body.
distractorExplanations.d: Nutrition still drives the calorie deficit needed for fat loss.

options.a: Inhale deeply and hold through the whole set
options.b: Breathe in rapidly and shallowly on each rep
options.c: Exhale fully before starting the lowering phase
options.d: Brace, then exhale through the sticking point

distractorExplanations.a: Prolonged breath-holding spikes blood pressure and is risky for many clients.
distractorExplanations.b: Rapid shallow breathing prevents a stable brace.
distractorExplanations.c: Exhaling before the lowering phase removes trunk support when the load is heaviest.

options.a: Frequency, intensity, time, type, volume, and progression
options.b: Flexibility, intensity, tempo, type, variety, and power
options.c: Frequency, interval, training load, type, velocity, pace
options.d: Fitness, intensity, time, technique, volume, and posture

distractorExplanations.b: Flexibility, tempo, variety, and power are not the FITT-VP letters.
distractorExplanations.c: Interval, training load, velocity, and pace are not part of FITT-VP.
distractorExplanations.d: Fitness, technique, and posture are not the FITT-VP components.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-programming-007.explanation: FITT-VP means frequency, intensity, time, type, volume, and progression. ACSM uses it to structure aerobic, resistance, flexibility, and neuromotor prescriptions.

options.a: A week of 1RM testing to set new training loads
options.b: A planned drop in volume or intensity for recovery
options.c: A week off all exercise after an injury diagnosis
options.d: A week of extra volume to push past a plateau

distractorExplanations.a: Maximal testing adds stress; a deload reduces it.
distractorExplanations.c: A deload keeps some training; it is not injury rest.
distractorExplanations.d: Extra volume is an overreaching block, the opposite of a deload.

options.a: Standing on two feet on a firm floor with eyes closed
options.b: Single-leg stance on a firm floor with eyes open
options.c: Single-leg stance on foam while catching a ball
options.d: Tandem stance on a firm floor with arms crossed

distractorExplanations.a: Closing the eyes adds difficulty, but a two-foot base is still wide and stable.
distractorExplanations.b: A single leg on a firm surface lacks instability and reactive demands.
distractorExplanations.d: Tandem stance narrows the base but keeps both feet on a stable floor.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-programming-009.prompt: Which balance exercise is the most advanced progression?

options.a: 2–3 days a week, 8–10 exercises, starting at 1 set of 8–12
options.b: 5–6 days a week, 3 exercises, 5 sets of 3 reps at 90% 1RM
options.c: 1 day a week, 20 exercises, 3 sets to failure for each one
options.d: Daily sessions, 2 exercises, 10 sets of 15 reps each

distractorExplanations.b: Low-rep, high-set work is a strength block for trained lifters, not a novice start.
distractorExplanations.c: Once a week is too infrequent, and 20 exercises to failure is excessive for a novice.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily training of the same muscles leaves no recovery for a beginner.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-programming-010.prompt: For a healthy novice, ACSM's starting resistance-training guideline is closest to:
acsm-cpt-readiness-check-programming-010.explanation: ACSM suggests novices train each major muscle group 2–3 days a week with 8–10 multi-joint exercises, starting with one set of 8–12 repetitions and adding sets as they adapt.

options.a: Weighted sit-ups and machine crunches for high reps
options.b: Bridges, dead bugs, and bird dogs with control
options.c: Loaded Russian twists at end-range rotation
options.d: Hanging leg raises to failure each session

distractorExplanations.a: Loaded spinal flexion is harder on the spine and comes after basic stability.
distractorExplanations.c: End-range loaded rotation is an advanced, higher-risk movement.
distractorExplanations.d: Hanging leg raises need grip and hip-flexor strength most beginners lack.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-programming-011.prompt: Which core exercises are most appropriate for a beginner's first program?

options.a: Maximal strength through low-rep heavy lifting
options.b: Aerobic capacity through long steady-state work
options.c: Acceleration, change of direction, and reaction
options.d: Muscle hypertrophy through moderate-rep sets

distractorExplanations.a: Heavy low-rep work builds maximal strength, not agility.
distractorExplanations.b: Long steady work builds aerobic capacity.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypertrophy comes from resistance volume, not agility drills.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-programming-012.prompt: Speed, agility, and quickness drills primarily develop:

options.a: Stretch the calves and strengthen the tibialis anterior
options.b: Strengthen the chest with heavier bench press sets
options.c: Stretch the hamstrings and strengthen the hip flexors
options.d: Stretch the lats and chest; train mid and lower traps

distractorExplanations.a: Calf work addresses heel lift or foot turn-out, not the arms.
distractorExplanations.b: More chest loading reinforces the tightness that pulls the arms forward.
distractorExplanations.c: Hamstring and hip work targets pelvic position, not the shoulders.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-programming-013.prompt: A client's arms fall forward during an overhead squat. Which corrective approach fits best?

options.a: About 6–12 reps at moderate to heavy loads
options.b: About 1–5 reps at near-maximal loads each set
options.c: About 20–30 reps at very light loads per set
options.d: About 3–6 reps performed explosively

distractorExplanations.b: One to five heavy reps mainly builds maximal strength.
distractorExplanations.c: Very high reps with light loads target muscular endurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-rep explosive work trains power.

options.a: Lengthen muscles with long static stretches
options.b: Raise tissue temperature and rehearse movements
options.c: Pre-fatigue the target muscles before lifting
options.d: Lower heart rate before the working sets begin

distractorExplanations.a: Long static holds before lifting can briefly reduce force output.
distractorExplanations.c: Pre-fatigue reduces performance and is not the purpose of a warm-up.
distractorExplanations.d: A warm-up raises heart rate gradually; it does not lower it.

options.a: Muscles that only produce movement in the sagittal plane
options.b: Muscles that work together to stabilize and move a joint
options.c: Muscles that oppose the prime mover during an action
options.d: Muscles that attach to the same bone at both ends

distractorExplanations.a: Synergists can act in any plane; plane is not what defines them.
distractorExplanations.c: Muscles that oppose the prime mover are antagonists.
distractorExplanations.d: A muscle attaching to one bone at both ends could not move a joint.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-001.prompt: Synergist muscles are best described as:
acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-001.explanation: Synergists assist the agonist and help stabilize the joint so the intended movement happens efficiently. Antagonists oppose the movement, and stabilizers hold other segments still.

options.a: Coracoid process of the scapula
options.b: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus
options.c: Radial tuberosity
options.d: Olecranon process of the ulna

distractorExplanations.a: The coracoid process is an origin of the short head of the biceps, not its insertion.
distractorExplanations.b: The lateral epicondyle is the origin of the wrist extensors.
distractorExplanations.d: The olecranon is where the triceps inserts.

options.a: Muscular endurance: high reps, low load, short rest
options.b: Maximal strength: low reps, heavy load, long rest
options.c: Power: explosive reps with moderate load
options.d: Hypertrophy: moderate reps and moderate rest

distractorExplanations.b: Heavy low-rep work is a later phase once technique and tolerance are built.
distractorExplanations.c: Power training needs a strength base first.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypertrophy work usually follows an initial endurance and technique phase.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-003.prompt: For a deconditioned client, which resistance-training emphasis usually comes first?
acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-003.explanation: New or deconditioned clients usually start with lighter loads, higher repetitions, and shorter rest to build muscular endurance and technique before moving to hypertrophy, strength, or power work.

options.a: Iliopsoas
options.b: Gluteus maximus
options.c: Rectus femoris
options.d: Tensor fasciae latae

distractorExplanations.a: The iliopsoas is the primary hip flexor.
distractorExplanations.c: The rectus femoris flexes the hip and extends the knee.
distractorExplanations.d: The TFL assists hip flexion and abduction.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-004.prompt: Which muscle is the primary agonist for hip extension?

options.a: Ligament
options.b: Bursa
options.c: Cartilage
options.d: Tendon

distractorExplanations.a: Ligaments connect bone to bone.
distractorExplanations.b: Bursae are fluid sacs that reduce friction.
distractorExplanations.c: Cartilage covers joint surfaces and cushions them.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-006.prompt: Which connective tissue attaches muscle to bone?

options.a: Slow-twitch, oxidative, and fatigue-resistant
options.b: Fast-twitch, glycolytic, and quick to fatigue
options.c: Fast-twitch fibers recruited first at low effort
options.d: Slow-twitch fibers used mainly for maximal lifts

distractorExplanations.b: Fast-twitch glycolytic fibers are Type IIx.
distractorExplanations.c: Low-effort tasks recruit slow-twitch fibers first, following the size principle.
distractorExplanations.d: Maximal lifts rely heavily on Type II fibers.

options.a: Heavy squats and jump squats on separate days
options.b: A light plyometric drill followed by a 1RM test
options.c: A heavy lift paired with a similar explosive move
options.d: Isometric holds followed by long steady cardio

distractorExplanations.a: Separating the lifts on different days removes the pairing effect.
distractorExplanations.b: A 1RM test is a test, not a contrast training pair.
distractorExplanations.d: Isometrics and steady cardio do not train power.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-009.prompt: Complex (contrast) training for power typically pairs:
acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-009.explanation: Complex training pairs a heavy strength exercise with a lighter, high-velocity exercise for the same pattern, such as a squat followed by a jump, to use post-activation potentiation.

options.a: Serratus anterior and pectoralis minor
options.b: Upper trapezius and levator scapulae
options.c: Pectoralis major and anterior deltoid
options.d: Rhomboids and middle trapezius

distractorExplanations.a: Serratus anterior and pectoralis minor protract the scapula.
distractorExplanations.b: Upper trapezius and levator scapulae elevate the scapula.
distractorExplanations.c: Pectoralis major and anterior deltoid move the humerus, mainly in horizontal adduction; they do not retract the scapula.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-science-010.prompt: Which muscles concentrically retract the scapula?

options.a: Stabilize the lumbar spine by raising intra-abdominal pressure
options.b: Flex the trunk as the prime mover during sit-ups and crunches
options.c: Rotate the trunk as the prime mover during cable woodchops
options.d: Extend the lumbar spine as the prime mover during deadlifts

distractorExplanations.b: The rectus abdominis is the prime mover for trunk flexion.
distractorExplanations.c: The obliques are the prime movers for trunk rotation.
distractorExplanations.d: The erector spinae extend the spine.

options.a: It is fully shortened with sarcomeres overlapping
options.b: It is stretched to the end of its range of motion
options.c: Actin and myosin overlap optimally near rest length
options.d: It is contracting at the fastest possible velocity

distractorExplanations.a: When fully shortened, filaments overlap too much and force drops.
distractorExplanations.b: When overstretched, too few cross-bridges can form.
distractorExplanations.d: Force falls as shortening velocity rises (force–velocity relationship).

options.a: Oxidative system using carbohydrate
options.b: Oxidative system using fatty acids
options.c: Fast glycolysis producing lactate
options.d: ATP–PC (phosphagen) system

distractorExplanations.a: Aerobic metabolism is too slow to meet the demand of a maximal 10-second effort.
distractorExplanations.b: Fat oxidation is the slowest ATP pathway.
distractorExplanations.c: Glycolysis rises after the first several seconds but does not dominate this short effort.

options.a: Is the primary mover producing the desired joint action
options.b: Relaxes to allow the desired joint action to happen
options.c: Assists the prime mover in producing the joint action
options.d: Holds nearby joints steady while the movement happens

distractorExplanations.b: The antagonist relaxes and lengthens to allow the action.
distractorExplanations.c: A muscle that assists the prime mover is a synergist.
distractorExplanations.d: Muscles that hold nearby joints steady are stabilizers.

options.a: Collaborative exploration of ambivalence and motivation
options.b: Direct advice on the fastest way to reach client goals
options.c: Clear consequences when the client misses sessions
options.d: Detailed education on health risks of inactivity

distractorExplanations.b: MI evokes the client's own reasons rather than leading with advice.
distractorExplanations.c: Consequences and pressure increase resistance; MI avoids them.
distractorExplanations.d: Education has a place, but MI centers the client's own motivation.

options.a: Increasing sweat rate so the body cools more efficiently
options.b: Reducing plasma volume and raising cardiovascular strain
options.c: Lowering heart rate at a given workload during exercise
options.d: Increasing blood volume available to the working muscles

distractorExplanations.a: Dehydration reduces sweating capacity and raises core temperature.
distractorExplanations.c: Heart rate rises at a given workload when plasma volume falls (cardiovascular drift).
distractorExplanations.d: Fluid loss lowers blood volume; it does not increase it.

options.a: Did you complete all of your workouts this week?
options.b: Would you like to add one more session next week?
options.c: What got in the way of your workouts this week?
options.d: Was the last session too hard or about right?

distractorExplanations.a: This invites a yes or no answer, so it is closed.
distractorExplanations.b: This is a yes/no question even though it is polite.
distractorExplanations.d: Offering two choices limits the answer; it is a closed question.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-behavior-003.prompt: Which is an example of an open-ended coaching question?

options.a: Build a low-carbohydrate meal plan and track glucose
options.b: Suggest a calorie target and remind the client to test
options.c: Provide sample diabetic menus from a trusted website
options.d: Refer to a dietitian or physician for nutrition therapy

distractorExplanations.a: A disease-specific meal plan is medical nutrition therapy, outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Setting targets for a diabetic client is clinical nutrition therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: Handing out diabetic menus is still individualized medical nutrition advice.

options.a: Prioritize sleep, planned progression, and nutrition
options.b: Use daily ice baths after every training session
options.c: Take a full week off training after every 2 weeks
options.d: Stretch statically for 20 minutes after each session

distractorExplanations.b: Frequent cold water immersion can blunt strength and hypertrophy gains.
distractorExplanations.c: This is far more rest than typical periodization requires.
distractorExplanations.d: Static stretching has little effect on recovery or soreness.

options.a: Keeps session notes brief to limit what can be subpoenaed
options.b: Screens clients, documents sessions, and stays in scope
options.c: Relies on the gym's insurance to cover any client injury
options.d: Uses a waiver so no further screening or records are needed

distractorExplanations.a: Thin notes weaken a trainer's defense; clear records reduce liability.
distractorExplanations.c: Facility insurance may not cover an independent trainer's negligence.
distractorExplanations.d: Waivers do not replace screening, documentation, or reasonable care.

options.a: Moderate intake improves muscle protein synthesis
options.b: Alcohol calories are not stored as body fat
options.c: Excess intake can impair recovery, sleep, and diet
options.d: Alcohol rehydrates well after an endurance session

distractorExplanations.a: Alcohol reduces muscle protein synthesis after training.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol provides 7 kcal/g, and those calories can contribute to fat gain.
distractorExplanations.d: Alcohol is a diuretic and can worsen post-exercise dehydration.

options.a: Share general healthy eating guidance; refer MNT to an RD
options.b: Design meal plans for clients with high blood cholesterol
options.c: Recommend an elimination diet for suspected food allergies
options.d: Adjust a client's carbohydrate intake to manage diabetes

distractorExplanations.b: Planning meals to treat a disease is medical nutrition therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: Elimination diets for allergies need clinical supervision.
distractorExplanations.d: Managing diabetes through diet is clinical care for an RD or physician.

options.a: Dietary fat
options.b: Carbohydrate
options.c: Dietary protein
options.d: Ketone bodies

distractorExplanations.a: Fat is oxidized aerobically and is too slow for glycolysis.
distractorExplanations.c: Protein contributes little energy during intense exercise.
distractorExplanations.d: Ketones are oxidized aerobically and do not fuel glycolysis.

options.a: About 0.5–0.8 g/kg/day, at or below the RDA
options.b: About 3.0–4.0 g/kg/day for all active adults
options.c: About 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day, by goals and training
options.d: About 0.8 g/kg/day regardless of training load

distractorExplanations.a: This is at or below the sedentary RDA and too low for most active adults.
distractorExplanations.b: Intakes this high exceed what is needed for most exercisers.
distractorExplanations.d: 0.8 g/kg is the sedentary RDA; active adults usually need more.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-behavior-010.prompt: Protein intake for many regularly exercising adults falls near:

options.a: Long-term outcome goals without weekly targets
options.b: Motivational quotes posted in the training area
options.c: Rewards that are given only after the final goal
options.d: Specific action plans and self-monitoring

distractorExplanations.a: Outcome goals without weekly actions give no clear next step.
distractorExplanations.b: Quotes may inspire briefly, but they are not a behavior-change technique.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for the end goal removes the regular reinforcement that builds habits.

options.a: The law requires it or the client gives consent
options.b: The client's physician calls to ask for details
options.c: A family member asks about the client's progress
options.d: The gym manager asks to review client files

distractorExplanations.b: Sharing with a physician still requires the client's consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Family members have no right to the client's information without consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Managers need a legitimate business reason and policy basis, not casual access.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-behavior-012.prompt: A CPT may disclose a client's private information when:

options.a: Recommend supplements that are third-party tested
options.b: Share general evidence and refer clinical questions
options.c: Sell supplements only if the client asks for them
options.d: Suggest doses based on the client's body weight

distractorExplanations.a: Testing reduces contamination risk, but recommending products still stretches scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Selling products creates a conflict of interest and is not evidence-based guidance.
distractorExplanations.d: Individual dosing is clinical advice outside CPT scope.

options.a: Simple, Motivating, Achievable, Rewarding, Tracked
options.b: Specific, Meaningful, Active, Reviewed, Targeted
options.c: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, Time-bound
options.d: Strategic, Measured, Agreed, Realistic, Timed

distractorExplanations.a: These words are not the standard SMART acronym.
distractorExplanations.b: Meaningful, Active, Reviewed, and Targeted are not SMART terms.
distractorExplanations.d: Strategic and Agreed are not in the standard acronym.

options.a: Offering a money-back guarantee on weight-loss results
options.b: Advertising body-transformation photos from past clients
options.c: Setting prices individually based on each client's income
options.d: Clear contracts, transparent pricing, and honest claims

distractorExplanations.a: Results guarantees overpromise; outcomes depend on many factors outside the trainer's control.
distractorExplanations.b: Client photos need written consent and can mislead if results are not typical.
distractorExplanations.c: Undisclosed individual pricing is not transparent.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-behavior-015.prompt: Which business practice is most professional for a personal trainer?

options.a: Run a submaximal cycle test and stop at 85% of HRmax
options.b: Start light walking and reassess symptoms in two weeks
options.c: Check resting HR and BP, then test if both are normal
options.d: Defer testing and refer him for medical evaluation

distractorExplanations.a: A submaximal test still loads the heart of a client with possible cardiac symptoms.
distractorExplanations.b: Starting exercise before evaluation ignores a red-flag symptom.
distractorExplanations.c: Normal resting values do not rule out exertional chest symptoms.

options.a: Reduces short-term rises from activity, caffeine, or stress
options.b: Lets the cuff warm to body temperature for a steady reading
options.c: Is the time an automatic monitor needs to calibrate itself
options.d: Allows blood to pool in the legs for a lower reading

distractorExplanations.b: Cuff temperature does not affect the reading.
distractorExplanations.c: Monitors do not need a calibration period between clients.
distractorExplanations.d: The goal is a stable resting value, not an artificially low one.

options.a: Lower-body muscular endurance from total step count
options.b: Aerobic fitness from post-test heart rate recovery
options.c: Anaerobic power from the fastest stepping cadence
options.d: Balance from the number of missteps during the test

distractorExplanations.a: Cadence is fixed by a metronome; step count is not the score.
distractorExplanations.c: The fixed cadence makes this a submaximal aerobic test, not an anaerobic one.
distractorExplanations.d: Missteps are not scored; the result is the one-minute recovery heart rate.

options.a: The trainer's certifications and their expiry dates
options.b: That the waiver removes liability for all injuries
options.c: Activities, risks, and the right to stop at any time
options.d: The expected results and a timeline to reach them

distractorExplanations.a: Credentials may be shared, but they are not the core of informed consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Consent documents do not remove liability for negligence.
distractorExplanations.d: Promising results is not part of consent and can mislead the client.

options.a: Low bone density and a higher fracture risk
options.b: Reduced flexibility of the lumbar spine
options.c: Lower resting metabolic rate than average
options.d: Visceral fat and cardiometabolic disease

distractorExplanations.a: Waist size does not assess bone density.
distractorExplanations.b: Waist circumference does not measure flexibility.
distractorExplanations.c: Waist size is a disease-risk marker, not a measure of metabolic rate.

options.a: Take one reading per site to avoid compressing tissue
options.b: Average readings that fall within the protocol's range
options.c: Use the highest reading at each site for safety
options.d: Measure on the left side of the body for accuracy

distractorExplanations.a: A single reading is unreliable; protocols require repeat measurements.
distractorExplanations.c: Choosing the highest value biases the estimate upward.
distractorExplanations.d: Most US protocols, including ACSM's, use the right side of the body.

options.a: Getting physician clearance before any exercise begins
options.b: Completing a maximal exercise test before training
options.c: Starting light to moderate exercise and progressing
options.d: Starting at vigorous intensity to establish a baseline

distractorExplanations.a: Healthy asymptomatic clients do not need clearance for light to moderate exercise.
distractorExplanations.b: A maximal test is not required for an asymptomatic client starting moderate exercise.
distractorExplanations.d: ACSM suggests starting inactive clients at light to moderate intensity and progressing gradually.

options.a: Shoulder and thoracic spine mobility
options.b: Hip flexor and quadriceps flexibility
options.c: Ankle dorsiflexion range of motion
options.d: Hamstring and low-back flexibility

distractorExplanations.a: Shoulder mobility is assessed with tests such as the back scratch test.
distractorExplanations.b: Hip flexor length is checked with the Thomas test.
distractorExplanations.c: Ankle dorsiflexion is assessed with a knee-to-wall test.

options.a: Can talk in full sentences but cannot sing
options.b: Can sing comfortably while keeping pace
options.c: Can speak only a few words between breaths
options.d: Cannot speak at all without stopping

distractorExplanations.b: Being able to sing suggests light intensity.
distractorExplanations.c: Only a few words at a time suggests vigorous intensity.
distractorExplanations.d: Inability to speak suggests near-maximal effort.

options.a: A 45-year-old with controlled hypertension on medication
options.b: A 60-year-old walker with a knee replacement last year
options.c: A 52-year-old with uncontrolled hypertension and syncope
options.d: A 38-year-old with type 1 diabetes and good control

distractorExplanations.a: Controlled hypertension usually allows training with monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: A healed joint replacement may limit impact but is not a cardiac red flag.
distractorExplanations.d: Well-controlled diabetes needs glucose monitoring, not deferral of all testing.

options.a: Resting HR, maximal HR, and the target intensity
options.b: Resting HR, age, and the client's body weight
options.c: Maximal HR, blood pressure, and target intensity
options.d: Resting BP, age, and the client's RPE rating

distractorExplanations.b: Body weight is not part of the HRR formula.
distractorExplanations.c: Blood pressure is not used in the Karvonen formula.
distractorExplanations.d: The formula uses heart rates, not BP or RPE.

options.a: Is inactive, over 45, and has two CVD risk factors
options.b: Has known heart disease and signs or symptoms
options.c: Is active, healthy, and wants to add vigorous work
options.d: Has a BMI over 30 but no other known health issues

distractorExplanations.a: Risk-factor counts and age were removed from the 2015 algorithm.
distractorExplanations.c: Active clients without disease or symptoms can progress without clearance.
distractorExplanations.d: Obesity alone is not a clearance trigger in the current algorithm.

options.a: Moderate loads for 6–8 reps with long rest periods
options.b: Machine exercises only for the first three months
options.c: Bodyweight exercises only until they lose weight
options.d: 12–15 reps at light to moderate load with control

distractorExplanations.a: Six to eight reps is heavier than a deconditioned older adult needs at first.
distractorExplanations.b: Machines help, but restricting to machines for months is unnecessary.
distractorExplanations.c: Weight loss is not a prerequisite for adding external resistance.

options.a: 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity
options.b: 75 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity
options.c: 300 minutes a week of vigorous aerobic activity
options.d: 30 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity

distractorExplanations.b: 75 minutes is the vigorous-intensity equivalent, not the moderate target.
distractorExplanations.c: 300 minutes is the upper moderate range for added benefit, not the vigorous minimum.
distractorExplanations.d: 30 minutes a week is far below the recommended minimum.

options.a: Hold the lifter's elbows to guide the bar path
options.b: Assist if the bar stalls or the client asks
options.c: Keep hands on the bar through every rep
options.d: Stand beside the bench to watch the arch

distractorExplanations.a: Spotting at the elbows gives no control of the bar.
distractorExplanations.c: Touching the bar on every rep changes the lift and hides true effort.
distractorExplanations.d: A bench spotter stands at the head to reach the bar, not at the side.

options.a: Low reps at heavy loads with 3–5 minutes rest
options.b: Moderate reps at moderate loads to failure
options.c: 15–20 or more reps with short rest intervals
options.d: Explosive reps at light loads with full rest

distractorExplanations.a: Heavy low-rep work with long rest builds maximal strength.
distractorExplanations.b: Moderate reps to failure mainly target hypertrophy.
distractorExplanations.d: Explosive reps with full rest train power.

options.a: Walking lunges with light dumbbells
options.b: Reverse lunges onto a soft balance pad
options.c: Lateral lunges with the arms overhead
options.d: Split squats holding a stable support

distractorExplanations.a: Walking lunges add forward motion, which increases balance demand.
distractorExplanations.b: An unstable pad makes balance harder, not easier.
distractorExplanations.c: Lateral movement and arms overhead both increase the balance challenge.

options.a: About 3 days a week, then progress
options.b: About 5–7 days a week from week one
options.c: About 1 day a week for the first month
options.d: Every other week until fitness improves

distractorExplanations.b: Daily sessions from week one progress too quickly for a beginner.
distractorExplanations.c: One day a week is too little to produce meaningful adaptation.
distractorExplanations.d: Training every other week does not provide a regular stimulus.

options.a: Use heavy loads with few reps to keep sets short
options.b: Use moderate loads and cue continuous breathing
options.c: Avoid all upper-body exercises during training
options.d: Train only seated to prevent any rise in BP

distractorExplanations.a: Heavy low-rep sets encourage breath-holding and BP spikes.
distractorExplanations.c: Upper-body work is appropriate with sensible load and breathing.
distractorExplanations.d: Position does not prevent BP from rising; load and breathing matter most.

options.a: Match work and rest periods at 1:1 from the first session
options.b: Use all-out efforts and let the client choose the rest
options.c: Start with short work bouts and longer recovery periods
options.d: Replace steady cardio fully with intervals right away

distractorExplanations.a: Equal work and rest is too demanding for most sedentary clients at first.
distractorExplanations.b: All-out efforts are inappropriate for a sedentary beginner.
distractorExplanations.d: Intervals should be added gradually alongside a steady aerobic base.

options.a: VO2max through all-out one-minute repeats
options.b: Running economy through hill sprint drills
options.c: Aerobic base through long, easy distance runs
options.d: Lactate threshold and sustained race pace

distractorExplanations.a: Short all-out repeats target VO2max and anaerobic capacity, not threshold.
distractorExplanations.b: Hill sprints build power and economy; tempo runs build threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: Easy long runs build aerobic base at a lower intensity than tempo work.

options.a: Lowering reps and raising load, with longer rest
options.b: Raising reps and lowering load, with less rest
options.c: Keeping reps the same and adding more sets
options.d: Switching to explosive reps with light loads

distractorExplanations.b: Higher reps with lighter loads shift toward endurance.
distractorExplanations.c: More sets at the same reps adds volume, not a strength emphasis.
distractorExplanations.d: Explosive light loads train power, which usually follows a strength phase.

options.a: Deep loaded squats to rebuild cartilage strength
options.b: Cycling, swimming, and pain-monitored strength
options.c: Running on soft surfaces to reduce joint load
options.d: Rest until symptoms fully resolve, then train

distractorExplanations.a: Deep loaded squats can aggravate an arthritic knee, and loading does not rebuild cartilage.
distractorExplanations.c: Running is still high impact, even on soft surfaces.
distractorExplanations.d: Rest leads to deconditioning; appropriate activity helps OA symptoms.

options.a: A heavy upper-body session to rest the legs
options.b: Complete rest with no movement for two days
options.c: Light walking or mobility work at low effort
options.d: Moderate squats to flush out the soreness

distractorExplanations.a: A heavy session is not recovery, even for different muscles.
distractorExplanations.b: Complete inactivity is not needed after a normal hard session.
distractorExplanations.d: More squatting adds stress to the same tired muscles.

options.a: Grip strength needed to hold the bar
options.b: Knee flexion at the start of the pull
options.c: Hip hinge range at the top of the lift
options.d: Excessive lumbar flexion under load

distractorExplanations.a: Grip is trained separately; the hinge does not affect grip.
distractorExplanations.b: Some knee flexion is part of a correct conventional setup.
distractorExplanations.c: The hinge is a movement pattern, not something to reduce at lockout.

options.a: Leg strength, aerobic base, and recovery days
options.b: Upper-body strength and short sprint intervals
options.c: Maximal leg strength with little aerobic work
options.d: Long daily hikes with no rest days scheduled

distractorExplanations.b: Upper-body strength and sprints do not match hiking demands.
distractorExplanations.c: Hiking needs endurance as well as strength.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily long hikes without rest risk overuse and fatigue before the trip.

options.a: Repeat the session to speed up the adaptation
options.b: Reduce volume and prioritize recovery
options.c: Switch to heavy concentric-only lifting
options.d: Tell the client it is a muscle strain

distractorExplanations.a: Repeating the same eccentric load on sore muscles delays recovery.
distractorExplanations.c: Heavy loading of sore muscles is not recovery.
distractorExplanations.d: Trainers do not diagnose injuries; DOMS is expected after new eccentric work.

options.a: Lengthens while producing tension
options.b: Holds its length while producing tension
options.c: Relaxes while the triceps pulls
options.d: Shortens while producing tension

distractorExplanations.a: Lengthening under tension is an eccentric action.
distractorExplanations.b: Constant length under tension is isometric.
distractorExplanations.c: The biceps is the agonist here; it does not relax during the lift.

options.a: An eccentric action as the chest lowers
options.b: A concentric action as the chest lowers
options.c: An isometric action at the bottom only
options.d: No action; the triceps controls the descent

distractorExplanations.b: Concentric means shortening, which happens while pushing up.
distractorExplanations.c: The pecs work through the whole descent, not only at the bottom.
distractorExplanations.d: The pecs control the descent together with the triceps and anterior deltoid.

options.a: Adaptations continue at the same rate indefinitely
options.b: Adaptations match the specific demands imposed
options.c: Adaptations are reversed when training stops
options.d: Adaptations differ between individual clients

distractorExplanations.a: Adaptation slows as clients get fitter; this is not SAID.
distractorExplanations.c: Losing gains after stopping is the reversibility principle.
distractorExplanations.d: Individual differences are a separate principle.

options.a: Aerobic metabolism of carbohydrate
options.b: Anaerobic glycolysis producing lactate
options.c: Oxidation of fatty acids
options.d: The ATP–PC (phosphagen) system

distractorExplanations.a: Aerobic metabolism is too slow for a 6-second maximal sprint.
distractorExplanations.b: Glycolysis grows after several seconds but does not dominate a 6-second sprint.
distractorExplanations.c: Fat oxidation is the slowest energy pathway.

options.a: Lower heart rate allowing longer filling time
options.b: Greater venous return and stronger contraction
options.c: Reduced blood volume from sweating
options.d: Increased peripheral vascular resistance

distractorExplanations.a: Heart rate rises during exercise, so filling time shortens.
distractorExplanations.c: Sweat loss reduces blood volume and tends to lower stroke volume.
distractorExplanations.d: Resistance in working muscle falls during exercise; higher resistance would reduce stroke volume.

options.a: Slow contraction speed and high oxidative capacity
options.b: Moderate speed with both oxidative and glycolytic use
options.c: Fast contraction and high force, with rapid fatigue
options.d: Recruitment first during low-intensity activity

distractorExplanations.a: Slow, oxidative fibers are Type I.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixed oxidative-glycolytic fibers are Type IIa.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-intensity work recruits Type I fibers first.

options.a: Increased heart rate alone with no change in vessels
options.b: Constriction of arteries supplying the working muscle
options.c: Reduced cardiac output sent to the skeletal muscles
options.d: Local vasodilation and redirected cardiac output

distractorExplanations.a: Heart rate helps, but local vessel changes are key to redirecting flow.
distractorExplanations.b: Working muscle vessels dilate; constriction would reduce flow.
distractorExplanations.c: Cardiac output rises during exercise, and more of it goes to muscle.

options.a: Unaccustomed eccentric muscle damage
options.b: Lactic acid building up in the muscles
options.c: Dehydration during the downhill run
options.d: Depleted muscle glycogen stores

distractorExplanations.b: Lactate clears within about an hour and does not cause soreness days later.
distractorExplanations.c: Dehydration does not explain soreness peaking 24–72 hours later.
distractorExplanations.d: Low glycogen causes fatigue, not delayed soreness.

options.a: Lower blood pressure by reducing venous return
options.b: Raise intrathoracic pressure and blood pressure
options.c: Reduce spinal stability during the heavy lift
options.d: Increase oxygen delivery to the working muscles

distractorExplanations.a: Blood pressure rises during the strain; it can drop after release.
distractorExplanations.c: Breath-holding increases trunk stiffness and spinal stability.
distractorExplanations.d: Breath-holding does not improve oxygen delivery.

options.a: Raise maximal heart rate, so zones are set too low
options.b: Increase blood pressure during resistance training
options.c: Blunt the heart rate response, so zones are unreliable
options.d: Cause heart rate to spike during the warm-up only

distractorExplanations.a: Beta-blockers lower, not raise, maximal and exercise heart rate.
distractorExplanations.b: Beta-blockers usually lower blood pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: They blunt heart rate throughout exercise, not just the warm-up.

options.a: Rapid strength gains followed by a short plateau
options.b: Muscle soreness lasting 24–72 hours after training
options.c: Increased appetite during high-volume weeks
options.d: Persistent fatigue, falling performance, poor sleep

distractorExplanations.a: Gains followed by a plateau are normal training responses.
distractorExplanations.b: Short-term DOMS is normal after new or hard sessions.
distractorExplanations.c: More appetite during heavy training is expected, not a sign of overtraining.

options.a: Storing elastic energy in a quick eccentric pre-stretch
options.b: Holding a long isometric pause before the takeoff
options.c: Using a slow eccentric phase to recruit more fibers
options.d: Relying on passive ligament stretch for rebound

distractorExplanations.b: A long pause lets stored elastic energy dissipate.
distractorExplanations.c: The cycle depends on a fast eccentric phase, not a slow one.
distractorExplanations.d: The effect comes from muscle and tendon, not ligaments.

options.a: The oxygen deficit at the start of exercise
options.b: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC)
options.c: The ventilatory threshold during the session
options.d: Maximal oxygen uptake reached during the session

distractorExplanations.a: The oxygen deficit occurs at the start of exercise, not afterward.
distractorExplanations.c: Ventilatory threshold is an intensity marker during exercise.
distractorExplanations.d: VO2max is peak uptake during exercise, not recovery consumption.

options.a: Suggest early-morning sessions to fit the schedule
options.b: Explain the health risks of staying inactive
options.c: Design a short program the client can start now
options.d: Reflect the conflict and explore small changes

distractorExplanations.a: Offering solutions first skips exploring the client's ambivalence.
distractorExplanations.b: Leading with risks can increase resistance in MI.
distractorExplanations.c: Prescribing before exploring ambivalence is not the MI first step.

options.a: Refer to the agreement and clarify paid boundaries
options.b: Provide a few free plans to keep the relationship
options.c: Stop replying to messages without any explanation
options.d: Offer a discount only if the client posts a review

distractorExplanations.b: Ad hoc free work blurs boundaries and sets expectations.
distractorExplanations.c: Ignoring the client is unprofessional; boundaries should be stated clearly.
distractorExplanations.d: Trading discounts for reviews can be deceptive marketing.

options.a: Drink less soda and more water starting next month
options.b: Swap one 20-oz soda for water on weekdays for 4 weeks
options.c: Cut out soda completely and never drink it again
options.d: Try to reduce soda intake as much as possible

distractorExplanations.a: This lacks a measurable amount and a clear timeline.
distractorExplanations.c: An all-or-nothing goal is rarely realistic for a first step.
distractorExplanations.d: This is vague and has no measure or deadline.

options.a: Removing all flexibility from the weekly schedule
options.b: Restarting at full volume after any missed week
options.c: Planning ahead for high-risk times such as travel
options.d: Setting stricter goals after each missed session

distractorExplanations.a: Rigid schedules break easily; relapse prevention builds in flexible options.
distractorExplanations.b: Jumping back to full volume after a lapse raises soreness and dropout risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Stricter goals after a lapse increase pressure and the chance of quitting.

acsm-cpt-readiness-check-behavior-019.prompt: Which strategy best helps a client prevent a lapse from becoming a relapse?
acsm-cpt-readiness-check-behavior-019.explanation: Relapse prevention identifies high-risk situations such as travel, illness, or schedule changes and plans alternatives in advance, so one missed session does not end the habit.

options.a: Speak with the parents before taking any action
options.b: Document concerns and wait for more evidence
options.c: Report only if the minor asks for help directly
options.d: Follow state mandated-reporter laws and policy

distractorExplanations.a: Confronting parents can put the child at further risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Reporting laws require acting on reasonable suspicion, not proof.
distractorExplanations.c: Children often do not disclose; the duty applies on reasonable suspicion.

options.a: Listen, avoid diagnosing, and refer to a professional
options.b: Build a structured meal plan to reduce binge triggers
options.c: Suggest skipping meals after a binge to balance calories
options.d: Increase training volume to offset the extra calories

distractorExplanations.b: Meal plans for disordered eating need an RD or clinician.
distractorExplanations.c: Compensatory restriction can reinforce the binge cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Compensatory exercise can worsen disordered eating.

options.a: Drink only when thirsty, even in hot weather
options.b: Start well hydrated and replace sweat losses
options.c: Drink a liter of water just before starting
options.d: Use sports drinks only, with no plain water

distractorExplanations.a: Thirst can lag behind fluid needs during long sessions in heat.
distractorExplanations.c: A large bolus just before exercise is poorly absorbed and uncomfortable.
distractorExplanations.d: Water is fine for most sessions; sports drinks are optional.

options.a: Offer a moderate deficit plan with weekly check-ins
options.b: Agree only if the client's physician signs off first
options.c: Decline restrictive plans and refer to an RD or therapist
options.d: Focus on exercise and let the client manage their diet

distractorExplanations.a: Any prescribed deficit is risky with an eating disorder history and outside scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Physician sign-off does not bring clinical diet design into CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Staying silent misses a chance to refer a client with a known risk.

options.a: Long-term goals reviewed once every six months
options.b: Comparing progress with more experienced clients
options.c: Frequent changes of program to keep things new
options.d: Achievable short-term goals and self-monitoring

distractorExplanations.a: Rare reviews give few chances for mastery experiences.
distractorExplanations.b: Comparison with advanced exercisers can lower self-efficacy.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequent changes prevent the client from mastering skills.

options.a: Exercises, loads, client responses, adverse events
options.b: The client's full medical history from their doctor
options.c: Only attendance and payment for each session
options.d: Only the exercises completed in that session

distractorExplanations.b: Full medical records are not routine session notes.
distractorExplanations.c: Attendance and billing leave out safety and progression details.
distractorExplanations.d: Exercises without loads and responses do not support safety or continuity.

options.a: Train at a lighter intensity and monitor closely
options.b: Postpone the session and address safety concerns
options.c: Continue with machines only to reduce fall risk
options.d: Ask the client to hydrate and then begin training

distractorExplanations.a: Training an impaired client at any intensity is unsafe.
distractorExplanations.c: Machines do not remove the risks of impairment.
distractorExplanations.d: Water does not reverse alcohol impairment.

options.a: Using the same program template for every client
options.b: Avoiding discussion of culture to stay neutral
options.c: Respecting values and adapting communication
options.d: Assigning goals based on a client's background

distractorExplanations.a: One template ignores differences in values and needs.
distractorExplanations.b: Avoiding the topic can miss needs such as dress or dietary practices.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigning goals by background relies on stereotypes.

options.a: Is thinking about change within the next 6 months
options.b: Has been exercising regularly for over 6 months
options.c: Began exercising regularly within the last 6 months
options.d: Plans to start within 30 days and takes small steps

distractorExplanations.a: Thinking about change within six months is contemplation.
distractorExplanations.b: Six or more months of regular exercise is maintenance.
distractorExplanations.c: Recent regular exercise is the action stage.

options.a: Respond briefly with facts and no client details
options.b: Post the client's attendance record to correct it
options.c: Ask other clients to post reviews to outweigh it
options.d: Reply in detail to explain the client's situation

distractorExplanations.b: Sharing client records breaches confidentiality.
distractorExplanations.c: Soliciting reviews to bury criticism is deceptive.
distractorExplanations.d: Detailed replies risk exposing private client information.

options.a: A replacement for goal setting and self-monitoring
options.b: Accountability, encouragement, and shared norms
options.c: Competition that ranks clients by their results
options.d: Advice from friends in place of professional input

distractorExplanations.a: Support works alongside goals and monitoring, not instead of them.
distractorExplanations.c: Ranking can discourage beginners; it is not the main support mechanism.
distractorExplanations.d: Friends' advice does not replace professional guidance.
